captions.text: Night on the prairie. Grass as far as you can see.
The sun rises. Every blade gets bright, full light.
Out here, wind blows, and rain comes and goes.
Now a forest. Drop from the treetops…

On the forest floor, it's dim, cool, and damp.
A fern? Down here, where the sun barely reaches?
Its fronds spread wide and flat. Why that shape?
Two homes, two very different plants. Why?
Let's compare plants from two different places.

words: A trait that helps a living thing survive in its environment.
A feature of a plant or animal, like leaf shape, root depth, or stem thickness.
Something that helps a plant survive or reproduce better than others in its environment.
The place where a living thing lives and gets what it needs to survive.
To stay alive through hard conditions, like cold, drought (a long dry time), shade, or other challenges.
A difference in traits between plants or animals of the same type.

parts.title: Two Very Different Homes
parts.html:
A mountain forest and an open grassland are very different places to live. In a forest, tall trees block much of the sunlight. The soil is rocky and stays damp. It can get very cold.

Out in a grassland, sunlight is everywhere. Wind blows steadily. Rain comes and goes, and the soil can dry out for weeks.

parts.title: Traits Are Solutions
parts.html:
A fern on the shady forest floor has wide, flat fronds. Those broad leaves catch every bit of light that filters through the trees. That trait is a solution to the problem of shade.

A prairie grass has thin, tough leaves and roots that go deep, sometimes deeper than you are tall. That root system is a solution to dry seasons. It can reach water far underground when the surface dries out.

parts.title: The Right Trait for the Right Place
parts.html:
A trait gives an advantage when it solves a problem in that specific place. Deep roots are an advantage in a dry grassland. They are far less useful in a wet forest, where water is already near the surface.

Plants with traits that fit their place survive and make seeds or spores. Plants without them often don't.

compare.title: Which leaf shape handles the wind?
compare.look: Two real plant parts, each on a lit specimen tray. Specimen A is a fern frond from a shady forest floor. Specimen B is prairie grass from an open, windy field. Under the trays are two paper models for a test: a wide sheet of paper and a thin paper strip.

compare.testDo: Drag the wide sheet under one tray and the thin strip under the other, or tap each one, then tap a tray. Press Turn on the wind. Then swap them and press it again.
compare.disclaimer: This is a model. Paper isn't alive, but the idea is the same: a wide, flat shape catches a lot of wind. A thin, narrow shape lets wind slip past.

Awide.text: The wide sheet, shaped like this fern frond, flapped hard and ripped. Out in the open, wind is rough on wide leaves.

Astrip.text: The thin strip bent and sprang back. But this fern frond is wide and flat, not thin. Try the wide sheet here.

Bstrip.text: The thin strip, shaped like these grass leaves, bent in the wind and sprang right back.

Bwide.text: The wide sheet flapped and ripped. But these grass leaves are thin, not wide. Try the thin strip here.

compare.frame: This ___ is ___, so in a strong wind it would ___.
compare.claimLead: This plant has leaves that are
compare.claimMid: so in an open, windy field it would

curator.A: Wide and flat → torn by strong wind. On the forest floor, trees block the wind, and wide fronds catch the little light that gets through. That's an advantage in the shade, not out in the open.
curator.B: Thin and narrow → bends and springs back. Prairie grass lives where the wind blows all day. Thin, tough leaves bend instead of tearing, and the sun is bright, so the grass doesn't need wide leaves to catch light.

compare.missFeat: Look at {label} again. Are the leaves wide and flat, or thin and narrow?
compare.missClaim: Think about your test. What happened to each shape in the wind?
compare.done: Bigger leaves aren't always better. A wide leaf is an advantage in the shade, but out in the open wind, thin leaves do better.

after.kicker: 🎬 Behind the scenes · Built for wind
after.alt: Tall, thin prairie grass stems and seed heads against a blue sky
after.html: Big bluestem, a prairie grass, can grow taller than a grown-up. Scientists say its long, thin leaves and stems bend in the prairie wind instead of breaking. Its seed head splits into three parts, so people nicknamed it "turkey foot."

wall.title: Drop from the treetops to the forest floor
wall.look: A cutaway (a slice) of a forest, from the treetops down to the ground. It is a model. Each layer is a level of the forest, with its own plants and its own amount of light. The brass dial on the left shows which level you are at.
wall.do: First, make a prediction. Then brush the glowing layer: drag across it (or tap it again and again) until the plant shows.

predict.q: As you go down from the treetops to the forest floor, will there be more light, or less?
predict.mine: Your prediction: {p}. Let's go down and find out.
predict.confirm: You predicted less light. The evidence agrees: each layer of leaves blocked more sunlight, and the plants changed too.
predict.change: You predicted more light. The evidence changed that idea: each layer of leaves blocked more sunlight, so the floor was the darkest.

wall.skyAlt: Green, tree-covered mountains under a blue sky with clouds
wall.locked: Brush the level above first. The elevator goes down, one level at a time.
wall.first: Brush the glowing top layer. Drag across it (or tap it again and again).
wall.next: Going down, where it's darker. Brush Level {n}.
wall.endText: Look at the line. The treetops get full sun. Each layer of leaves below blocks more light, so the forest floor is the dimmest place of all.
wall.rule: In a forest, each level gets less light than the one above it. The plants at each level have traits that fit how much light reaches them.

mix.q: A sunflower loves bright, open sun. Would it grow well on the forest floor, next to the fern?

options.t: Yes. Any plant can grow anywhere if it gets water.
options.miss: Water isn't the only thing plants need. The forest floor is deep shade. A sun-loving plant wouldn't get enough light.

options.t: No. The forest floor is deep shade. A plant built for bright sun wouldn't get enough light there.
options.ok: Yes! A trait only helps in the right place. The fern fits the shade. The sunflower fits the open sun.

wow.title: A prairie's hidden half
wow.alt: An old drawing of prairie plants with their roots reaching far below the ground, next to a ruler in feet
wow.caption: Prairie plants and their roots, drawn by scientist John Weaver in 1919. It's a drawing, made from roots he dug up.
wow.html:
Scientist John Weaver spent years digging up prairie plants, root and all. He found that most of a prairie is hidden underground.

Scientists have measured switchgrass roots, a prairie grass, 8 to 11 feet deep. That's about as deep as a basketball hoop is high!
wow.insetCap: Big bluestem, a prairie grass. Its roots can reach 6 to 7 feet.

keyIdea: A trait is an adaptation when it gives a plant a survival advantage in its environment. The same trait that helps a plant in one place may be useless, or even harmful, somewhere else.

quiz.q: A fern on the forest floor has very wide, flat leaves. Why is this trait a useful adaptation?

options.t: Wide leaves help the fern store extra water during dry spells.
options.miss: Think about the fern's environment first. The forest floor is shady. Which leaf shape helps gather light in the shade?

options.t: Wide leaves help the fern catch dim, filtered light in the shade.
options.ok: ⭐ Exactly right! Shade is the fern's main challenge. Wide leaves catch every bit of dim light that filters through the trees.

options.t: Wide leaves make the fern harder for animals to eat.
options.miss: Think about the fern's environment first. The forest floor is shady. Which leaf shape helps gather light in the shade?

quiz.q: Grassland grasses often grow very deep roots. What challenge does this help them survive?

options.t: Too much shade from tall trees nearby.
options.miss: What's the biggest challenge for plants in an open grassland? Think about water, and what happens to the soil when it hasn't rained in a while.

options.t: Long dry seasons when the soil near the surface dries out.
options.ok: ⭐ Yes! Grasslands don't have much shade, but they do have dry seasons. Deep roots can reach water far underground when the surface dries out.

options.t: Too much rain that floods the soil.
options.miss: Deep roots don't fix floods. What's the biggest challenge in an open grassland? Think about water when it hasn't rained in a while.

quiz.q: Which of these is the best example of a survival advantage?

options.t: A plant that has colorful red and purple leaves.
options.miss: An advantage has to actually help a plant survive a challenge. Which option gives the plant a better chance of staying alive?

options.t: A plant whose roots can reach deep groundwater during a long dry season.
options.ok: ⭐ Good thinking! Deep roots that reach water during a drought give a plant a real advantage. More of those plants survive and reproduce.

options.t: A plant that grows more slowly than every other plant nearby.
options.miss: An advantage has to actually help a plant survive a challenge. Which option gives the plant a better chance of staying alive?
